Thank you for submitting your article "KymoButler, a deep learning software for automated kymograph analysis" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Vivek Malhotra as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Jeff Urbach (Reviewer #1).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

The manuscript by Jakobs et al. describes a fully automated approach to analyze kymographs based on deep learning. The software can run on both uni- and bidirectional kymographs. The code is freely available and the tool itself is also available via a web application. This is an important state of-the-art contribution as kymographs are notoriously difficult to obtain and to automate.

Essential revisions:

We are impressed with the substantial improvements to the analysis tool and the presentation in the revised manuscript. We all agree that KymoButler is a promising tool for the field. Nevertheless, some issues remain and should be addressed.

1) The authors have shown that the current version of the software can manage unidirectional and bidirectional movements. But, the capabilities of the software should be tested more thoroughly, both on synthetic and also on "real" data. For instance:

– Synthetic data: the limit of systems performances should be explored by varying density of tracings and signal/noise ratio. Moreover, the authors should also comment on the similarities and differences of synthetic data to real kymographs.

– Real data: the tool must be tested on several examples of different real situations presented (Rab11, mitochondria, microtubule plus-ends), distinct form the training data, and average performance should be quantified against manual expert tracing and best-performing available tool.

Since the authors already have a lot of manually annotated kymographs, they could remove some of them from the training set and get hard numbers on the performance of KymoButler on such data.

In addition, for both synthetic and real data, quantitative comparison should go as far as the end result that people seek to obtain from kymographs: average directionality,% of reversals, average speed, processivity, pause duration, etc. These quantitative parameters should be compared between Kymobutler, manual expert tracing and automatic alternatives in order to evaluate how the difference in tracing detection affects the final measurements.

2) The authors should state clearly in Introduction and Discussion what can and cannot be done with their software.

Considering that biological objects move in a stochastic 3D environment, the first paragraph of the Introduction should state explicitly which classes of motions are appropriate for kymographs and for KymoButler, respectively. It is not clearly described in the current version.

What a " stationary path" means should be explained.

In addition, it would be helpful to the user to know how KymoButler manages the stochastic versus directed motions as well as the constraints on the frequency of changes in direction. These points should be added in the Discussion.

3) It also appears that KymoButler's usability can be further improved and that some issues in the program should be fixed.

For instance, when an error occurs there is no possibility to try again, but instead one has to go back to previous screen, drag the input files over again, remember the old sensitivity threshold, submit again and hope for the best. Likewise, there is no possibility to simply change the sensitivity once you see the oversegmented results. One has to go back, drag all the data over, and repeat. Considering the allowed image size, simple thresholding should be fast enough to be interactive in the browser.

From a visual inspection, it is unclear how sensitivity parameter affects the outcome. It appears that the less sensitive setting (-1) does not pick some faint traces, and also breaks trajectories in pieces, resulting in a similar trace number as at the medium sensitivity setting.

results.result: KymoButler is a Deep Learning-based software built on U-Net architecture comprising two specialized segmentation modules (unidirectional and bidirectional), a classification module, and a decision module. The software was trained on 487 unidirectional and 79 bidirectional manually annotated kymographs plus synthetic data, generates trackness maps with values 0-1, has one adjustable threshold parameter (default 0.2), and completes analysis in 1-20 seconds per kymograph.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C24, C28-C35, C37-C41 provide comprehensive technical details about KymoButler's architecture, training data, and functionality. The modular design is well-documented with specific network architectures described in Materials and Methods (C99-C100), training datasets are quantified (C31-C32), and performance metrics are provided (C40). The implementation details are verifiable and internally consistent.

results.result: KymoButler performs as well as expert manual annotation on complex kymographs from diverse biological systems, achieving track F1 scores of 92% on unidirectional and 78% on bidirectional tracks, while being approximately 100x faster than manual analysis and outperforming existing automated software.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C26, C56-C58, C69-C71, C92 are strongly supported by quantitative benchmarking data presented in Figures 2-3. The F1 scores are calculated using well-defined metrics (track recall and precision), comparisons include both synthetic ground truth data and real biological data, and statistical tests are reported with p-values. The ~100x speed improvement is documented (C58, manual took 1.5 hr vs software <1 min for 10 kymographs).

results.result: KymoButler outperformed Fourier filtering (KymographDirect) by ~30% on unidirectional kymographs and wavelet filtering by 20% on bidirectional kymographs. Edge detection performed poorly on bidirectional data. The main advantage of KymoButler over filtering approaches was its ability to bridge track gaps and resolve line crossings.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C84-C89 are supported by systematic benchmarking experiments shown in Figures 2-3. Quantitative comparisons are provided with specific performance differences (30% and 20%), and the limitations of alternative methods are documented with visual examples (Figures 2C-D, 3C-D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The custom wavelet algorithm was implemented specifically for fair comparison (C59).

results.result: KymoButler correctly identified ~80% of tracks at SNR as low as 1.1 and at high particle densities (~70% image coverage), performing similarly to manual annotation under these extreme conditions. Performance decreased with decreasing SNR and increasing particle density for both KymoButler and manual annotation.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55, C76 are supported by systematic testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5. The SNR and particle density ranges are quantified, performance metrics are provided, and comparisons with manual annotation are included. The acknowledgment that performance degrades under extreme conditions (C76) demonstrates appropriate assessment of limitations.

results.result: The optimal binarization threshold for KymoButler's segmentation modules lies between 0.1-0.3 for both synthetic and published data, though the threshold depends on SNR and must be chosen based on specific biological applications and imaging conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C36, C74-C75 are supported by empirical testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4, which systematically evaluates threshold values from 0.05 to 0.5. The finding that optimal performance occurs in the 0.1-0.3 range is data-driven, and the acknowledgment of SNR-dependence (C75) is appropriate. However, the need for user optimization of this parameter somewhat limits the 'fully automated' claim.

results.result: KymoButler significantly speeds up data analysis and avoids unconscious bias compared to manual annotation, without suffering from inconsistency and laborious tracing that plague manual tracking.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C27, C93 regarding speed improvement are well-supported by timing data (manual: 1.5 hr vs KymoButler: <1 min for 10 kymographs, ~100x faster). The claim about avoiding bias (C9, C93) is reasonable for automated methods but is more of an inference than directly demonstrated—no experiments specifically tested for bias or consistency across multiple human annotators. The speed advantage is clearly demonstrated, but bias reduction is assumed rather than proven.

results.result: KymoButler successfully quantified mitochondria movement in neuronal dendrites, microtubule growth dynamics in axons, and in vitro dynamics of single cytoplasmic dynein proteins. The training data comprised similar biological systems, so KymoButler will perform best on similar data.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 are supported by demonstrations shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The training data composition is clearly described (C81), and the inference that performance will be best on similar data (C82) is reasonable. However, the generalizability claim in C83 (that it can be applied to most other fluorescence microscopy kymographs without modification) is speculative and not directly tested.

results.result: KymoButler was deployed as a web-based application at https://deepmirror.ai/kymobutler with an option for users to anonymously upload kymographs, which will be annotated and added to training data to improve the software.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C94 are factual statements about software deployment that are verifiable. Claim C95 describes a future improvement strategy that is reasonable but speculative—the improvement depends on future user uploads and subsequent annotation work. The deployment is documented, but the continuous improvement mechanism is a plan rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: Synthetic kymographs were generated with controlled parameters (300×300 pixels, SNR 1.2 for unidirectional and 1.4 for bidirectional data) and used for training and benchmarking. Performance metrics (track recall, precision, and F1 score) were calculated using well-defined overlap criteria allowing 3.2-pixel deviation from ground truth.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C109-C115 describe the synthetic data generation and evaluation methodology in detail. The parameters are clearly specified, the metrics are mathematically defined, and the approach is reproducible. The 3.2-pixel tolerance for deviation (C113) is reasonable given typical tracking uncertainties. The methodology is sound and well-documented in Materials and Methods.

results.result: Synthetic kymographs reproduce real kymograph complexity only to some degree due to homogeneous backgrounds, no artifacts, and no varying particle intensity. Manual annotation deviated by up to 20% from ground truth on synthetic data, indicating that deviations from manual annotation should not automatically be interpreted as errors.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 appropriately acknowledge limitations of synthetic data and variability in manual annotation. The 20% deviation of manual annotation from ground truth (C91) is documented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, providing important context for interpreting performance comparisons. This demonstrates good scientific practice in recognizing limitations.

results.result: KymoButler can potentially be applied to most kymographs from time-lapse fluorescence microscopy without modifications, and the approach could be extended to 3D/4D tracking problems using higher-dimensional FCNs, which has great potential for human-like performance on biological and medical tracking problems.
results.evaluation: Claims C83, C96-C98 are speculative (marked as SPECULATION in evidence_type). While C83 predicts broad applicability, this is not systematically tested beyond the training data domains. Claims C96-C98 discuss future extensions to higher-dimensional problems, which are reasonable extrapolations but not demonstrated. These represent promising future directions rather than established results.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on kymographs, their applications in biology, limitations of existing analysis tools, and the success of machine learning approaches in biological image analysis. Existing kymograph tools require manual supervision, perform well only on simple unidirectional motion, and most kymographs are still analyzed manually.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C10-C23, C72, C77-C78 provide literature context supported by appropriate citations. These background claims establish the motivation for developing KymoButler. The characterization of existing tools' limitations (C4, C14, C15, C77) is supported by citations and later demonstrated through benchmarking. The statements about ML success in biology (C18-C23) are well-cited.

results.result: The network architecture uses standard building blocks (batch normalization, leakyReLU) previously employed in Google's Inception and U-Net architectures. The classification module processes 64×64 pixel inputs, segmentation modules require input dimensions as multiples of 16, and training was performed on NVIDIA GPUs.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C106, C108 describe technical implementation details that are standard practices in deep learning (C102-C104 are general knowledge about neural network components). The architectural constraints (C106) follow from U-Net design. The hardware specifications (C108) are factual. These are well-established technical details appropriately documented.
